parole.testo: From Classical Syriac ܐܦܣܩܘܦܐ (ʾeppisqoppā) or a variant thereof, whence Persian سکوبا (sokubâ) might have been derived via Middle Persian *uskōpā, a borrowing of Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos).
Via Classical Syriac ܐܣܛܘܪܟܐ (ʾesṭurkā) from Ancient Greek στύραξ (stúrax).
From Classical Syriac ܐܢܩܪܕܝܐ (ʔanaqardīyā), from Ancient Greek ἀνακάρδιον (anakárdion).
From Classical Syriac ܐܢܩܗܠܝܣ / ܐܢܩܠܣܐ / ܐܢܩܠܝܣ, from Ancient Greek ἔγχελυς (énkhelus).

parole.significato: awqiyyah (ounce), a unit of weight in Egypt: 37 grams (one twelfth ratl)
parole.testo: Probably through Classical Syriac ܐܘܢܩܝܐ (ʾūnqīyā) from Ancient Greek οὐγγία (oungía), οὐγκία (ounkía), from Latin uncia (“ounce, twelfth part”), from ūnus (“one”). Cognate with English ounce.
Borrowed from Classical Syriac ܟܣܝܪܝܢ (ksīrīn), from Ancient Greek ξηρίον (xēríon, “medicinal powder”).

Most likely from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion), probably through Classical Syriac ܐܘܢܓܠܝܘܢ (ʾewwangellīōn) or a variant thereof, though also Ge'ez ወንጌል (wängel) or unattested Old South Arabian have been suggested as the immediate source.
From Classical Syriac ܒܰܪܕܽܘܢܳܐ (barḏūnā), from Ancient Greek βουρδών (bourdṓn), from Latin burdō, further etymology possibly Gaulish.

Borrowed from Classical Syriac ܒܽܘܢܳܐ (būnā), which, attested as “barley soaked in water”, underwent a meaning development in 14ᵗʰ-century Yemen due to brewages of sundry appetizing beverages, less likely in view of the pungent fish-sauce بُنّ (bunn), but from the picture of barley grains to the cof
Derived from ثَلَاثَة (ṯalāṯa, “three”), after Classical Syriac ܬܠܝܬܝܘܬܐ (tlīṯāyūṯā), Ancient Greek τριάς (triás) and Latin trīnitās.
From Classical Syriac ܓܶܢܛܝܢܳܐ (genṭyānā, “gentian”), from Ancient Greek γεντιανή (gentianḗ, “gentian”), allegedly after Gentius of Illyria discovering its use.

parole.significato: vervain (Verbena gen. et spp., especially Verbena officinalis)
parole.testo: A science translation calque of Classical Syriac ܪܥܝܐ ܕܝܘܢܐ (reʿyā də-yawnē), which is depending on the meaning of the first word “meadow of doves”, “kit of doves”, “food of doves”, apparently the Arabic translators took the “fodder” meaning as this is what Arabic رِعْي (riʕy) means—unless the Arabi
From Classical Syriac ܙܡܪܓܕܐ (zəmargaḏā, zəmarraḡdā), from earlier ܐܙܡܪܓܕܐ (ʾezmarraḡdā), from Ancient Greek σμᾰ́ραγδος (smắragdos). Doublet of زُمُرُّد (zumurrud).
Borrowed from Classical Syriac ܙܽܘܙܦܴܐ (zūzp̄ā), from Ancient Greek ζίζυφον (zízuphon). Also directly as زَيْزَفُون (zayzafūn).

Borrowed from Classical Syriac ܣܘܿܦܝܺܣܛܳܐ (sōp̄isṭā, “sophist”) or its nisba derivation ܣܘܿܦܝܺܣܛܳܝܳܐ (sōp̄isṭāyā, “sophistic”) from Ancient Greek σοφιστής (sophistḗs) and + ـَاء (-āʔ, feminine ending, sometimes for Aramaic emphatic state) + ـِيّ (-iyy, nisba, expresses relation or pertinence).

parole.significato: a literal counterbalance, counterpoise, standard weight
parole.testo: From Classical Syriac ܣܹܝܩܘܿܡܵܐ (sēqōmā), from Ancient Greek σήκωμᾰ (sḗkōmă).
Borrowed from Classical Syriac ܣܱܠܽܘܪܴܐ (sallūrā, “catfish”), from Ancient Greek σίλουρος (sílouros).
From Aramaic צַפּוֹן / ܨܦܘܢ (ṣappōn), from Ancient Greek σάπων (sápōn), from Latin sāpōnem, accusative of sāpō, from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ.

parole.significato: weather (usually used for short period meteorological changes)
parole.testo: From Classical Syriac ܛܟܣܐ (ṭekkəsā), from Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”).

parole.significato: form, mould, last (for casting shapes by it)
parole.testo: From Classical Syriac ܩܠܒܝܕ (/⁠*qālobīḏ⁠/, “last”), from Ancient Greek καλοπόδιον (kalopódion, “last”), diminutive of καλόπους (kalópous, “last”), compound of κᾶλον (kâlon, “wood”) and πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: lycanthrope; the bestial form of a werewolf
parole.testo: From Classical Syriac ܩܢܛܪܘܦܘܣ (qanṭropos), from Ancient Greek λυκάνθρωπος (lukánthrōpos).
From Classical Syriac ܩܷܦܱܠܷܐܘܳܢ (qeppalleʾōn, “sum”), from Ancient Greek κεφάλαιον (kephálaion, “sum”).

From Classical Syriac ܩܦܠܘܛܐ (qap̄lūṭā, qap̄lōṭā) adapted from Ancient Greek κεφαλωτόν (kephalōtón, “headed”) after πράσον (práson, “leek”) found in the Materia medica during the science translation movement.
From Classical Syriac ܩܷܠܴܝܬܴܐ (qellāṯā, qellāyṯā), ܩܷܠܻܝܬܴܐ (qellīṯā), from Ancient Greek κελλίον (kellíon), from Latin cella.
From Classical Syriac ܟܠܩܝܕܝܣ (/⁠*kalqidīs⁠/), from Ancient Greek χαλκῖτις (khalkîtis, “containing copper”), derived from χαλκός (khalkós, “copper”).
Borrowed from Classical Syriac ܩܢܕܠܐ (qandēlā), borrowed from Ancient Greek κανδήλη (kandḗlē).

Multiple confounded etymologies: * Via Classical Syriac ܩܶܢܛܪܳܘܢ (qenṭrōn) from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “center”), from the idea of an arch vaulting a central point. * From Classical Syriac ܩܛܰܪܬܴܐ (qəṭartā, “binding, node, conjunction; specifically also bridge”) from the root ܩ ܛ ܪ related
From Classical Syriac ܩܝܩܐܣ (qīqās), ܩܝܩܘܣ (qīqōs), from Ancient Greek κηκίς (kēkís).
From Classical Syriac ܩܝܣܘܪܐ, ܩܝܣܪܐ, ܩܣܪܐ, from Ancient Greek κίσσηρις (kíssēris).

parole.significato: caper (Capparis gen. and especially Capparis spinosa, as well as the edible buds from it)
parole.testo: From Classical Syriac ܩܦܪ (qappar, qappār, “caper-bush”) or Classical Syriac ܟܦܪ (kappar, kappār), considered from Ancient Greek κάππαρις (kápparis) of uncertain likely Asian origin. For the variation a ⇌ ā in Aramaisms, compare سُكَّر (sukkar), سُكَّار (sukkār, “bolt-lock”) and قُنْبَر (qunbar), قُ

parole.significato: chestnut (Castanea gen. et spp. and Aesculus spp.)
parole.testo: In some variants borrowed from Classical Syriac ܩܣܛܢܝܐ (qasṭāniyā) from Ancient Greek κᾰστᾰ́νειᾰ (kăstắneiă), in others directly from Ancient Greek κᾰ́στᾰνᾰ (kắstănă).
Borrowed from Classical Syriac ܟܠܫܐ (kelšā), borrowed from Ancient Greek χάλιξ (khálix), possibly borrowed from Pre-Greek.

parole.significato: a type of administrative division, translated as “district” or “province”, notably instituted by the Umayyad Caliphate…
parole.testo: From Classical Syriac ܟܘܪܐ (kōrā), from Ancient Greek χώρᾱ (khṓrā).

From Classical Syriac ܡܪܰܓܳܢ (margān, “pearl-like”), from ܡܰܪܓܳܢܺܝܬܳܐ (margānīṯā, “pearl”), from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs, “pearl”), an Iranian borrowing. For the meaning development compare Arabic مَرْو (marw, “odoriferous plants; Maerua crassifolia; pebble; flint; quartz”).

parole.significato: calcium silicate, dross or slags from glass
parole.testo: Borrowed from Classical Syriac ܡܫܚܩܘܢܝܐ (məšaḥ-qōnyā, literally “ointment of ashes”), from ܡܫܚܐ (mešḥā, “salve, unguent”) + ܩܘܢܝܐ (qōnyā, “ashes in general; lye from ashes and quicklime; glaze”) borrowed from Ancient Greek κονία (konía, “dust, ashes, scilicet potash, saltwort”).
Borrowed from Classical Syriac ܡܰܐܣܪܻܝܩܳܐ (māsārīqā), ܡܰܣܪܻ̈ܝܩܶܐ (masrīqē), ܡܶܗܣܳܐܪܻ̈ܝܩܶܐ (mēsārīqē), from Ancient Greek μεσαραϊκόν (mesaraïkón), from μεσάραιον (mesáraion).

From perhaps both Classical Syriac ܢܘܫܐ (nawšã, “coffin, sarcophagus; tomb, sepulchre”) and ܢܘܣܐ (nawsā, “charnel, repository for the dead”), derived from Ancient Greek νᾱός (nāós, “innermost part of a temple, sanctuary, or shrine”); applied historically by Greek sources to describe the burial chamb

Borrowed from Classical Syriac ܢܘܡܝܢ (nūmīn), from Ancient Greek νουμμίον (noummíon), diminutive of νοῦμμος (noûmmos) whence ܢܘܡܐ (nūmā), variant of νόμος (nómos), whence ܢܡܘܣܐ (nāmōsā) and نَامُوس (nāmūs).
From Classical Syriac ܗܠܝܘܢ (/⁠*helyōn⁠/), from Ancient Greek ἕλειον (héleion, “asparagus”), literally the neuter of ἕλειος (héleios, “of the marshland”).
